articles.title: PSMA Biology Through the Clinical Lens: Implications for Radioligand Therapy of Prostate Cancer with [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617.
articles.abstract: Prostate cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in men worldwide. While hormone therapy is effective in the early stages of advanced disease, multimodal approaches are often required as disease progresses, including radiotherapy, hormonal agents and chemotherapy. In metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), tumour cells become resistant to hormone therapy, resulting in poor survival outcomes despite systemic treatments. Among emerging therapies, radioligand therapy targeting prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) has shown promise. PSMA is a transmembrane glycoprotein highly expressed in prostate cancer cells, with minimal expression in normal tissues. This selective distribution enables precision targeting and minimises toxicity. The radiotheranostic agent [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 combines PSMA-617, a small molecule ligand, with the beta-emitting radioisotope 177Lutetium. This therapy has demonstrated efficacy in patients with mCRPC who have progressed after androgen receptor pathway inhibitors and taxane-based chemotherapy. Its regulatory approval in the USA, UK and Europe marks a pivotal advancement in prostate cancer management. Clinical trials such as TheraP, VISION and PSMAfore have established the role of [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 in mCRPC and its potential additive effects with other anti-tumour therapies are under investigation. Strategies to enhance PSMA expression may further improve therapeutic response. With no relevant drug-drug interaction risk, [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 may be safely considered for use in combination with other therapies, a key advantage for frail patients with mCRPC on polypharmacy. Post-treatment management remains a challenge and ongoing research aims to optimise long-term outcomes. This review provides a comprehensive update on [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-617 therapy, from molecular mechanisms to clinical application and outlines future directions in the treatment of advanced prostate cancer.

articles.title: Advancing extracellular vesicle therapeutics by chemical biology.
articles.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) possess favorable biocompatibility and diverse biological functions, making them promising platforms for therapeutic delivery. However, realizing their full delivery potential requires precise engineering of EVs with tailored functionalities. By bridging chemical tools and biological systems, chemical biology provides a versatile toolkit for the modular engineering of EVs. Here, we provide a systematic overview of recent progress in chemical biology-enabled EV engineering, with an emphasis on three main strategies including protein engineering, nucleic acid engineering, and glycoengineering. In this review, we discuss the design principles of representative approaches and assess their practical utility and performance. Particular attention is given to the integration of orthogonal engineering strategies to coordinate multiple delivery functions within a single EV platform. We further discuss emerging opportunities in multi-specific vesicular antibody design and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted engineering. By linking molecular engineering strategies with specific delivery requirements, this review provides a comprehensive chemical biology-based framework for the rational design of engineered EVs with tailored delivery functions.

articles.title: In vivo chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy: From mechanistic innovation to clinical translation.
articles.abstract: Conventional ex vivo chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy is limited by cumbersome manufacturing workflows, prohibitive costs and various treatment-related risks. In vivo CAR-T technology directly generates engineered cells within patients, conferring distinct advantages in operational simplicity, biosafety and clinical accessibility. This review systematically evaluates existing delivery platforms and classifies in vivo CAR-T into two core paradigms: persistent engineering and transient reprogramming, each featuring distinct properties tailored to different clinical indications. It further summarizes preclinical advances and clinical data covering hematological malignancies, solid tumors, autoimmune disorders and organ fibrosis, in which numerous investigational candidates have exhibited encouraging efficacy. Ultimately, five translational barriers summarized as the 5S challenges (specificity, stability, safety, suppression and scalability) and their matched optimization tactics are comprehensively discussed. This review provides a clinician-oriented decision matrix that links carriers selection to disease biology, and a 5S optimization framework to guide next-generation vector design. Collectively, these insights establish a translational roadmap for customizing in vivo CAR-T design to specific clinical indications and take a critical step toward realizing the full therapeutic potential of this disruptive modality.

articles.title: Patients with Chronic Inflammatory Diseases Can Experience Higher Exposure of Small Molecule Drugs than Healthy Volunteers: An Analysis of Recently Approved Drugs.
articles.abstract: Chronic inflammation has long been known to downregulate the activity of certain cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes-the main enzymes responsible for the phase I metabolism of many small molecule drugs-potentially leading to higher exposures in patients with chronic inflammatory diseases compared to healthy volunteers. Neglecting this potential difference in the pharmacokinetics can have several implications for dose translation from healthy volunteers to proof of concept studies in patients: sub-optimal design of dose-ranging studies and increased risk of adverse events due to overprediction of safety margins. Yet this disease-drug interaction has rarely been prospectively considered in drug development in the past. This review aims to quantify the extent of decreased (apparent) clearance in patients compared to healthy volunteers of small molecule drugs that were approved by the FDA in the past 15 years for important chronic inflammatory indications. Based on reported population pharmacokinetic analyses, 25% (5 of 20) of small molecule drugs approved for the selected indications showed a meaningfully higher area under the curve (AUC) by more than 25% in patients compared to healthy volunteers. As a common feature, all five drugs are primarily metabolized by CYP3A4 or CYP2C19 and for four of the five drugs, the contribution of metabolism to their elimination is more than 50%. These findings highlight the need to assess a drug's susceptibility to changes in the metabolic activity under chronic inflammation when translating dose predictions from healthy volunteers to patients.

articles.title: Venlafaxine in oncology: supportive-care evidence and emerging preclinical anticancer signals: a systematic review.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Venlafaxine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, has been investigated in oncology for several supportive care indications and, more recently, for potential anticancer activity. However, the available evidence remains fragmented across clinical and preclinical studies. OBJECTIVE: This systematic review aimed to synthesize the available evidence regarding the role of venlafaxine in oncology, including established supportive care applications and emerging anticancer potential. METHODS: A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science from database inception to 22 August 2026. Original clinical and preclinical studies evaluating venlafaxine in cancer populations or experimental cancer models were eligible. Clinical and preclinical evidence was synthesized separately using a narrative approach. Methodological quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute tools for clinical studies and the SYRCLE Risk of Bias tool for animal studies. RESULTS: 25 studies were included, comprising 23 clinical studies and 2 preclinical studies. The strongest clinical evidence supported venlafaxine for treatment-related hot flashes, particularly among breast cancer survivors receiving endocrine therapy, with the strongest randomized, placebo-controlled trial evidence showing significantly greater reductions with venlafaxine than placebo (P < 0.0001 for higher doses); within-group percentage reductions are also reported but should not be interpreted as treatment effects. Evidence for chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy was inconsistent, with potential benefit for acute oxaliplatin-related neurotoxicity but insufficient support for prevention or routine treatment of chronic CIPN. Evidence for other supportive care outcomes, including oral mucositis-associated pain, fatigue, sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and quality of life, was limited. Venlafaxine was generally well tolerated, although adverse effects varied by dose and comparator. Preclinical studies investigated anticancer activity, but not equivalently: one in melanoma models showed direct antiproliferative/pro-apoptotic effects of venlafaxine via JNK1/2-Nur77 signaling, whereas a colorectal cancer study showed only context-dependent antagonism of norepinephrine-driven tumor progression, with no significant effect of venlafaxine alone. No clinical evidence currently supports venlafaxine as a direct anticancer treatment. CONCLUSION: Venlafaxine has an established evidence-based role in supportive oncology for treatment-related hot flashes, whereas its role in CIPN and other supportive care indications remains uncertain. Emerging anticancer findings are limited to preclinical models and should be considered hypothesis-generating. Further randomized clinical trials are needed for supportive care indications, while additional mechanistic and preclinical validation is required before venlafaxine can be considered for clinical evaluation as an anticancer therapy.

articles.title: Repurposing the orphan drug nitisinone synergizes with sorafenib to sensitize immunotherapy-refractory MSS-CRC via metabolic stress-driven STING activation.
articles.abstract: Microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer (MSS-CRC) remains broadly refractory to immune checkpoint blockade, underscoring the need for strategies that convert immunologically "cold" tumors into therapy-responsive states. Here, we identify 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPD), the rate-limiting enzyme in tyrosine catabolism, as a modulator of sorafenib sensitivity in MSS-CRC. Pharmacological inhibition of HPD by the FDA-approved orphan drug nitisinone synergized with sorafenib across patient-derived organoids, human PBMC-tumor co-cultures, and immunocompetent orthotopic models. Mechanistically, nitisinone imposes strict glutaminolysis dependency, whereas sorafenib disrupts cRaf-MEK-ERK signaling to trigger proteasomal cMYC degradation and transcriptional repression of GLS1, thereby ablating compensatory glutamine anaplerosis. This dual metabolic blockade creates a synthetic lethal trap, provoking irreversible mitochondrial collapse and mtDNA release, which activates the cGAS-STING pathway and drives intratumoral infiltration of cytotoxic NK and CD8+ T cells. Critically, ρ⁰ cells and STING-deficient models confirm mitochondrial damage as the "trigger" of cell death and STING as the "amplifier" of antitumor immunity. In TCGA MSS-CRC cohorts, a double-low glutamine/tyrosine metabolic signature was associated with prolonged survival, enhanced cGAS-STING signaling, and immune-hot tumor features, findings corroborated by single-cell RNA-seq analyses. Finally, the triple combination of nitisinone, sorafenib, and anti-PD-1 therapy achieved superior antitumor efficacy with favorable tolerability in vivo. Collectively, our findings delineate a metabolic-mitochondrial-STING axis and support repurposing nitisinone as a promising translational strategy to sensitize MSS-CRC to immunotherapy.

articles.title: Repeated cocaine exposure and prolonged withdrawal drive morphological and molecular remodeling of hippocampal microglia in response to acute stress.
articles.abstract: Repeated cocaine exposure during adolescence disrupts physiological brain maturation, inducing persistent neuroplastic adaptations that evolve throughout withdrawal. Because stressful experiences are among the most powerful triggers of relapse during abstinence, uncovering how cocaine withdrawal affects the neurobiological mechanisms of stress adaptation and emotional responses remains a critical challenge in addiction research. Here, we investigated whether prolonged withdrawal from adolescent cocaine exposure alters hippocampal neuroimmune responses to a subsequent stressful challenge. Male adolescent rats received cocaine (5mg/kg, s.c.) for 15 consecutive days followed by a 14-day withdrawal period. At the end of withdrawal, animals were exposed to acute restraint stress (ARS) and assessed for anxiety-like behavior. Our findings demonstrate that prolonged withdrawal from adolescent cocaine exposure impairs emotional adaptation to acute stress, accompanied by persistent neuroimmune dysregulation across both central and peripheral compartments. Within the hippocampus, a key limbic hub integrating contextual drug-associated memories, emotional processes and stress adaptation, cocaine withdrawal altered microglial homeostasis while reshaping stress-responsive neuro-glial communication pathways in a region-specific manner, particularly the CX3CL1-CX3CR1 axis within the ventral subregion. Stress exposure revealed distinct microglial and synaptic, structural and molecular, adaptations in cocaine-withdrawn rats, characterized by the recruitment of a surveillance-like microglial phenotype and an altered pattern of neuron-microglia communication. These central alterations were accompanied by peripheral lymphopenia and a blunted lymphocyte response to the challenge. Together, these findings support the existence of a latent neuroimmune vulnerability induced by cocaine withdrawal that becomes apparent under challenging conditions potentially driving maladaptive stress processing.

articles.title: YAP/AP-1 Activation in Sebocytes Promotes CCL5-Dependent Perifollicular Macrophage Recruitment in Rosacea.
articles.abstract: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder in which macrophages have been increasingly implicated, yet the spatial basis and local cues of their recruitment remain poorly defined. Given the prominent perifollicular inflammatory changes in rosacea, we investigated whether sebocytes contribute to macrophage recruitment and the underlying mechanisms. Multiplex immunofluorescence combined with distance-stratified quantification demonstrated a preferential perifollicular distribution of macrophages around pilosebaceous units (PSUs) in human rosacea lesions. Integrated single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic analyses identified the C-C motif chemokine ligand 5 (CCL5)-C-C motif chemokine receptor 5 (CCR5) axis as a candidate mediator of sebocyte-macrophage crosstalk. Silencing CCL5 by small interfering RNA and CCL5 neutralization attenuated sebocyte-driven macrophage migration in vitro and reduced macrophage accumulation in vivo. Transcriptomic analysis of sebocytes further linked CCL5 expression to activation of Yes-associated protein (YAP)/activator protein-1 (AP-1) signaling. Consistently, pharmacological inhibition of YAP or AP-1 reduced CCL5 expression in sebocytes and alleviated erythema and macrophage infiltration in vivo. Furthermore, untargeted lipidomics uncovered profound metabolic reprogramming in sebocytes, characterized notably by the accumulation of cholesteryl esters. Bidirectional interventions via simvastatin and cholesterol loading confirmed that this lipid remodeling acts as an upstream driver of YAP nuclear translocation. Overall, our study identifies a PSU-centered inflammatory niche in rosacea and implicates lipid-driven, YAP/AP-1-associated sebocytic CCL5 upregulation in perifollicular macrophage recruitment, providing a rationale for further exploring sebocyte- and pilosebaceous unit-directed therapeutic strategies in rosacea.

articles.title: Overcoming technological and biological barriers to pulmonary mRNA delivery with lipid-polymer hybrid nanoparticles.
articles.abstract: Delivering mRNA to the lungs promises treatment of genetic, infectious and non-communicable lung diseases. Yet, conventional lipid nanoparticle formulations lack the stability needed to endure the harsh mechanical stress during nebulization. Additionally, once deposited in the respiratory tract, gene delivery systems may first have to overcome the mucus barrier, before actually transfecting the target cells. To overcome these challenges, we utilize lipid-polymer hybrid nanoparticles (LPH), merging the stability of pharmaceutical polymers with the transfection efficiency of cationic and ionizable lipids. LPH are produced in a robust microfluidic process, accomplish near-complete encapsulation efficiency, even after nebulization, and confer high transfection efficiency in A549 cells. To provide colloidal stability after aerosolization, we developed a coating strategy with hyaluronic acid (HA) and poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA), ensuring ideal nebulization stability by steric shielding. This formulation showed good transfection efficiency of air-liquid interface grown Calu-3 cells, producing and covered by mucus. The potential of LPH to deliver mRNA to mammalian cells was first shown in primary human lung fibroblasts in vitro and could also be confirmed after intratracheal administration to mice in vivo. Together, these findings validate LPH as a versatile and aerosolizable mRNA delivery platform, overcoming the key technological and biological barriers in pulmonary gene delivery.

articles.title: A modular nucleic acid-albumin biomolecular platform for multifunctional drug designs.
articles.abstract: The nanomedicine field has seen a paradigm shift towards multifunctional drug designs to maximise drug efficacy. Assembly of functionalised oligonucleotide (ODN) modules onto an albumin scaffold is an attractive solution offering a technological advancement in albumin-based drug delivery we apply in this work for a T-Cell Engager (TCE) and Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor (ICI) immuno-oncology combination. The "plug-and-play" modular approach was used to incorporate an anti-programmed cell death protein ligand 1 (anti-PD-L1) nanobody-ODN module onto a bispecific anti-EGFR x anti-CD3 scFv-albumin TCE fusion. Cys34 ODN site-specific conjugation on albumin allowed subsequent base-driven annealing of the complementary anti-PD-L1 nanobody-ODN module offering an easy and versatile alternative to established protein engineering approaches. The biomolecular components elements demonstrated effective binding of cellular targets in vitro, efficient PD-1/PD-L1 axis blockade and enhanced T-cell mediated cancer cell killing compared to single or separate combined treatments. Modular assembly on an albumin scaffold engineered with high neonatal Fc receptor affinity increased the circulatory half-life in humanised FcRn/albumin mice from 18.8 h to 26.6 h compared to wild type albumin sequences. This biomolecular assembly reflects the transition in the field towards multifunctional platforms exemplified in this work with an ICI and TCE combination promoting application for a range of functionalities and drug class combinations and offering programable half-life through inclusion of albumin sequences with different FcRn affinities.

Clitoria ternatea as a phytopharmacological resource: plant metabolites, mechanistic evidence, translational prospects, and safety considerations.
articles.abstract: Clitoria ternatea L. (Fabaceae; butterfly pea) is used in traditional medicine and is increasingly developed as a food colorant, functional beverage, botanical preparation, and source of peptide scaffolds. Previous reviews have separately emphasized ethnomedicine, flower extraction, anthocyanins, or cyclotides; however, the evidence has rarely been integrated according to preparation identity, study design, bioavailability, safety, and translational readiness. This structured critical narrative review updates the literature through 8 August 2026. PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar were searched using species-name and domain-specific terms. Primary studies were prioritized, and evidence was stratified as chemical/analytical, in silico, isolated-target or cell-based, animal, and human. Study interpretation considered taxonomic authentication, plant part, extraction and chemical characterization, dose, controls, duration, model relevance, adverse-event reporting, and exposure plausibility. The principal metabolite classes are ternatin anthocyanins, flavonol glycosides, phenolic acids, triterpenoids, sterols, and cyclotides. Chemical assays such as DPPH and ABTS support redox characterization but do not establish pharmacological or therapeutic efficacy. Neurobehavioral, anti-inflammatory, metabolic, antimicrobial, organ-protective, and cytotoxic signals are reported mainly in preclinical models, often using incompletely standardized extracts. Human evidence is restricted to small acute crossover studies and exploratory adjunctive studies, including a 2026 study of flower tea in people with type 2 diabetes and diabetic distress. Intact ternatins are orally absorbed in rats, but systemic exposure is modest and human pharmacokinetic data are unavailable; metabolite exposure, formulation effects, chronic toxicity, reproductive safety, cyclotide immunogenicity, and botanical-drug interactions remain insufficiently defined. Recent genomic and peptide studies strengthen the biotechnology relevance of cyclotides and butelase-1 but should not be conflated with the efficacy of crude botanical preparations. Overall, C. ternatea is a promising source of defined food, botanical, and peptide products, but therapeutic claims require authenticated materials, marker-based standardization, exposure-linked pharmacology, and adequately controlled clinical trials.

articles.title: The synergistic potential of combining PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors with conventional therapies in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
articles.abstract: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is associated with a poor prognosis, and the efficacy of conventional therapies (chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and surgery) remains limited. The advent of programmed death 1 (PD-1)/programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) inhibitors has substantially altered the treatment paradigm for ESCC. The combination of these immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) with conventional treatments demonstrates significant synergistic potential. Standard oncological regimens often center on chemotherapy, radiotherapy, surgery, or various combinations thereof. This synergy stems from complementary mechanisms: conventional therapies can induce immunogenic cell death, release tumor antigens, and remodel the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, thereby laying the groundwork for immunotherapy. In turn, PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors work by releasing the "brakes" on T cells, activating and enhancing the host anti-tumor immune response. This facilitates the elimination of residual cancer cells and establishes long-term immune surveillance. In conclusion, the combination of PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors with conventional therapy achieves a greater-than-additive ("1 + 1>2") effect and has evolved into a standard first-line treatment strategy for advanced/metastatic ESCC, substantially improving patient outcomes. Future research will focus on optimizing combination protocols, overcoming resistance, and precisely identifying patient populations most likely to benefit.

articles.title: The Patient Perspectives of Clinical Pharmacist Services in Hospitals and Clinics: A Focused Narrative Review of Qualitative Studies.
articles.abstract: Patient perspectives are highly important to ensure optimal patient care in hospitals or primary care settings. Clinical pharmacy services, in which clinical pharmacists provide direct patient care, are a relatively recent addition to healthcare and are increasing in scope and availability. In this focused narrative review, relevant qualitative studies describing patients' perspectives after the integration of clinical pharmacists into healthcare services were included. Patients described predominantly positive feedback, presented as facilitators. The facilitators described in studies were that patients felt safe, experienced clear communication and collaboration with pharmacists, increased their knowledge of medications, and appreciated pharmacists' time and availability. Occasionally, patients described challenges with the pharmacist or service, presented as barriers. The barriers were that patients were unfamiliar with the clinical pharmacists' role and services, lacked trust or experienced conflicting information, experienced a lack of patient-centredness, and some disagreed or had challenges with elements of the intervention. In conclusion, most perspectives represented positive facilitators that should be kept and protected in the future, with some barriers that can be overcome in the future for optimal patient care and development of clinical pharmacy services.

articles.title: Developing physiologically based pharmacokinetic models to understand lactation exposure to medications: Gaps in available data and call for action.
articles.abstract: Although a significant proportion of postpartum women use medication whilst breastfeeding, information regarding infant exposure to maternal medication via the breast milk is typically limited. In addition to growing pressures for the generation of clinical lactation data from regulators, interest in the use of alternative techniques, such as physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modelling, to support clinical studies in this underserved population is increasing. This is consistent with the current interest in model-informed drug development. For lactation models to contribute to clinical decision making, the uncertainties underpinning these models must be understood and minimized where possible. This review therefore aimed to investigate the breast milk distribution models used to support PBPK modelling in the lactation context and to characterize the sources and extent of uncertainty associated with these models. Three models were identified throughout the literature, termed as the Phase Distribution, Log-Transformed Phase Distribution, and Semi-Mechanistic models. Model performance, as compared against observed data, was broadly consistent between each of the three models but significant limitations were identified. Specifically, there is a paucity of clinical lactation data in which breast milk constituents are adequately defined to allow validation of mechanistic models; in vitro data inconsistently support model assumptions; and limited data have been generated using samples from a range of women to offer an understanding of population variability. These gaps in available data are clearly addressable, and further work should be conducted to better support the use of modelling and help address the inequities in safe access to medicine currently faced by women who breastfeed their infants.

articles.title: Role of TRPA1 channel modulation and therapeutic interventions in murine cutaneous injury: A systematic review.
articles.abstract: TRPA1 channels have gained prominence for their important role in the neurogenic inflammatory process and skin tissue repair. Our objective was to conduct a systematic review of the effects of TRPA1 receptor agonists and antagonists on the wound healing process in mice. Searches were conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase. We included in vivo murine studies focusing on the inflammatory response, cell signaling, and regeneration. Risk of bias and methodological quality were assessed using the Cochrane and SYRCLE tools (PROSPERO: CRD420261300663). After screening, 19 studies met the eligibility criteria. Our results showed that the use of channel antagonists drastically reduces edema, myeloperoxidase (MPO) enzyme activity, excessive infiltration of neutrophils and macrophages, and the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Interestingly, in TRPA1 knockout models, there was a delay in wound closure and a failure to heal, resulting in fibrotic scars. In contrast, when these channels were stimulated by topical agonists, they demonstrated accelerated wound healing and epidermal regeneration. Thus, TRPA1 plays a dual role in skin repair. While its therapeutic inhibition acutely attenuates exacerbated inflammation and edema, basal signaling and controlled activation of the receptor are essential for re-epithelialization, making this receptor a highly promising pharmacological target.

articles.title: Exploring the therapeutic role of Chinses herbal medicine in the recurrence rate of uterine fibroids after conservative surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Since surgery can only remove lesions of a larger size visible to the naked eye, the recurrence rate of uterine fibroids after surgery is high. In recent years, numerous scholars have found that traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) treatment is effective in reducing the recurrence rate of postoperative fibroids, as well as improving the clinical treatment rate, regulating serum hormone levels, reducing plasma viscosity, and promoting the restoration of uterine volume following surgery. Several randomized controlled trials have been undertaken on the prevention and treatment of postoperative recurrence of uterine fibroids using patented Chinese medicines and self-proposed formulations, such as Guizhi Fuling Pill, Xiaozheng decoction, Xiangleng pill, Zhengjia decoction, Xiaoliu decoction, Guizhi Jiliu pill, Huoxue Huayu formula, Huoxue Xiaozheng decoction, Shugan Sanjie decoction, Gongliuxiao capsule, Hongjin Xiaojie concentrated pill, and Jiawei Guizhi Fuling decoction. However, no study has systematically evaluated Chinese herbal medicine (CHM) in reducing the recurrence rate of uterine fibroids after surgery. AIM OF THE STUDY: This study aimed to conduct a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials of CHM for the prevention of postoperative recurrence of uterine fibroids, evaluating its efficacy and safety. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A comprehensive search was conducted on PubMed, Cochrane, Embase, Web of Science, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), VIP Information Database (VIP), WanFang Database, and China Biomedical Database (CBM) to identify randomized controlled clinical studies conducted up to March 2025 that examined the efficacy of CHM in treating patients with postoperative uterine fibroids. Two institutes were independently under-selected, and data were extracted and quality assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool. Meta-analyses were performed using Review Manager software 5.4, and forest plots were generated. The quality of evidence was assessed using GRADEpro 3.2.2. This study was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251000288). RESULTS: 16 trials were included in this study, and the postoperative recurrence rate after treatment was mainly analyzed. CHM treatment reduces postoperative recurrence rates in patients with uterine fibroids compared to the blank (6 trials, n = 588; OR (odds ratio) = 0.22; 95% CI (95% confidence intervals) = 0.14-0.34; I2 = 0%, p < 0.00001), conventional western medicine (CWM) (1 trial, n = 80; OR = 0.30; 95% CI = 0.09-0.93, p = 0.04), and combined CHM with CWM (9 trials, n = 959; OR = 0.29; 95% CI = 0.19-0.46; I2 = 0%, p < 0.00001). In addition, CHM is also effective in improving clinical efficiency, restoring serum sex hormone levels, lowering plasma viscosity, and reducing uterine volume. CHM is generally considered safe, with a low incidence of adverse reactions. CONCLUSION: CHM is effective in avoiding recurrence of uterine fibroids after surgery, excelling in terms of overall effectiveness, restoring female hormone levels, improving hemorheological indices, and promoting uterine recovery and safety. However, these findings are preliminary and still need to be validated by higher-quality studies.

articles.title: Occurrence of macrolide antibiotics in drinking water sources and their potential health risks.
articles.abstract: Macrolide antibiotics (MLAs) are widely utilized in both human and veterinary medicine. Their extensive use has led to ubiquitous contamination in aquatic environments, posing significant risks to public health and ecosystems. Despite their prevalence, comprehensive analyses of their environmental fate, diverse exposure pathways, and potential molecular toxicological mechanisms remain insufficient. This study systematically reviewed MLAs in global drinking water sources from 2005 to 2025 and their potential impacts on health. Using VOSviewer for bibliometric analysis, key research clusters focusing on ecological risks, antimicrobial resistance development, and health outcomes were identified. MLAs are frequently detected in surface and groundwater, with concentrations exceeding 1000 ng/L in specific regions, primarily influenced by seasonal variations and regional industrial activities. Additionally, we assessed how MLAs through the food chain into human dietary sources such as seafood and dairy products. Clinically, MLAs exposure correlates with a range of adverse health outcomes including cardiotoxicity (QT interval prolongation), hearing loss, obesity, and developmental defects. Five representative toxicity pathways were reviewed: mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired mitophagy/apoptosis, hERG potassium channel blockade, altered bile acid homeostasis, nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) inhibition, and oxidative stress. The evidence supporting these pathways varies across individual macrolides, and their relevance to exposure through drinking water remains uncertain. By identifying existing research gaps, this review establishes a robust scientific foundation for risk assessment and calls for enhanced oversight to mitigate the environmental and health risks associated with MLAs.

articles.title: Redox-Active Coumarin Derivatives: Chemico-Biological Mechanisms Linking Oxidative Stress, Mitochondrial Dysfunction and Regulated Cell Death.
articles.abstract: Coumarin derivatives are structurally diverse benzopyrone-based compounds with broad relevance to medicinal chemistry, redox biology, mitochondrial pharmacology and photobiology. Their biological effects are highly context-dependent and are shaped by substitution pattern, concentration, metabolic activation, intracellular localization, metal coordination and light exposure. This review critically examines the chemico-biological mechanisms through which coumarin derivatives influence oxidative stress signaling, mitochondrial function and regulated cell death. Particular emphasis is placed on the distinction between chemical radical-scavenging activity observed in simplified assays and biologically relevant redox modulation in cells. Although hydroxy- and methoxycoumarins may display antioxidant capacity in chemical systems, their cellular effects are more plausibly mediated through redox-sensitive signaling pathways, including NRF2/KEAP1/ARE, NF-κB and MAPK, and through modulation of enzymatic antioxidant defenses rather than direct stoichiometric scavenging of oxidants in vivo. Conversely, selected synthetic hybrids, metal complexes, mitochondria-targeted derivatives and photoactivatable coumarins may promote ROS/RNS accumulation, nitric oxide-related signaling, calcium dysregulation, mitochondrial membrane depolarization, cytochrome c release, apoptosis, ferroptosis-associated lipid peroxidation, autophagy-associated responses and photodynamic cytotoxicity. We also discuss how tumor-cell heterogeneity, basal redox state, NRF2 activity, NF-κB dependence, metabolic context and antioxidant reserve may determine whether coumarin exposure results in cytoprotection, growth inhibition or cell death. Finally, we evaluate major translational and toxicological barriers, including metabolic liability, hepatotoxicity, phototoxicity, photogenotoxicity, limited in vivo validation, insufficient target-engagement data and mechanistic overinterpretation of ROS-related endpoints. A more critical chemico-biological framework is required to guide the rational development of coumarin-based therapeutic, phototherapeutic and theranostic candidates.

articles.title: Liposomal and liposome-based formulations of pentacyclic triterpenoids in cancer nanomedicine: A critical appraisal of preclinical progress and future perspectives.
articles.abstract: Pentacyclic triterpenoids (PTs) comprise a broad range of multifunctional plant-derived compound that serve as attractive scaffolds for the development of anticancer drugs. Their modes of action range from triggering apoptosis to modulating oncogenic signaling pathways and the tumor microenvironment. Despite these therapeutic benefits, their clinical formulation has been limited by features such as poor bioavailability, hydrophobicity, high metabolism rates, and off-target toxicity. To overcome these limitations, liposomal nanocarriers provide a convenient delivery platform to improve pharmacokinetic profiles and enhance tumor-specific accumulation of PTs. This review provides a critical assessment of studies published between 2020 and 2026 on liposomal and liposome-based formulations of PTs for cancer therapy, focusing on the four PTs with the most extensive liposomal literature, namely betulinic acid (BA), ursolic acid (UA), glycyrrhizic acid (GA) and celastrol; studies of structurally related triterpenoids (e.g., betulin, oleanolic acid, lupeol, raddeanin A, platycodin D2) and of triterpenoid-containing extracts are considered as ancillary evidence. Approaches including liposome pegylation, ligand-mediated drug delivery, biotherapeutic surface modification, and co-delivery liposomal systems are reviewed. The main focus is on integrating formulation design with the physicochemical and pharmacokinetic properties of PTs. Moreover, the reviewed evidence indicates that liposomal encapsulation can improve cellular uptake and, in selected preclinical models, enhance antitumor activity and target-specific effects.

articles.title: Beyond LDL-C reduction: molecular pleiotropy and emerging therapeutic roles of statins.
articles.abstract: Statins rank among the most prevalent pharmacological treatments for the prevention and management of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, chiefly by inhibiting 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase and consequently reducing low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels. In addition to their recognized lipid-lowering properties, experimental, translational, and clinical research has uncovered various possible pleiotropic effects. These cholesterol-independent effects relate to the modulation of the mevalonate pathway and subsequent signaling molecules, which may affect endothelial function, nitric oxide availability, oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, atherosclerotic plaque stability, and thrombotic mechanisms. Nonetheless, the degree to which these processes yield clinically significant advantages apart from LDL-C lowering is still ambiguous. The clinical pharmacology of statins is examined, encompassing their pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic characteristics, molecular mechanisms of action, and novel therapeutic applications. Particular attention is directed at the molecular foundation and clinical relevance of statin pleiotropy in neurological conditions, metabolic disorders, inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, infectious illnesses, and cancer. The advantages and drawbacks of these prospective indications are rigorously assessed utilizing data from preclinical investigations, observational studies, randomized controlled trials, and meta-analyses. The evaluation additionally discusses safety factors, clinically significant drug-drug interactions, and the influence of pharmacogenomics in formulating individualized treatment approaches. Overall, statins have well-established cardiovascular benefits, whereas the clinical significance of their proposed pleiotropic effects and potential applications beyond cardiovascular disease varies across indications and remains incompletely established. Further high-quality, indication-specific clinical trials are needed to determine whether these effects provide additional therapeutic benefits and to define their appropriate clinical roles.

articles.title: Circadian-melatonin signaling in general anesthesia: molecular mechanisms and perioperative implications.
articles.abstract: Anesthesia and surgery are delivered to a temporally organized organism whose physiology is governed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, peripheral molecular clocks, and pineal melatonin signaling. This review synthesizes mechanistic, preclinical, and clinical evidence on how anesthetic agents, surgical stress, and the perioperative environment interact with circadian and melatonergic signaling, and on whether that interaction can be targeted therapeutically. In rodent and cellular studies, volatile and intravenous anesthetics alter clock function in an agent- and phase-dependent manner; proposed mechanisms include GABAergic and glutamatergic modulation of entrainment, transcriptional and chromatin-level repression of CLOCK-BMAL1/PER-CRY signaling, and metabolic coupling through CaMK-CREB, AMPK, SIRT1, and GSK-3β. These mechanisms have not been confirmed in humans. In patients, these effects are inseparable from surgical injury, opioids, fasting, inflammation, and disrupted light-dark exposure, all of which suppress melatonin amplitude, delay its onset, and promote internal desynchrony. Melatonin signals through MT1 and MT2 receptors to produce chronobiotic, anxiolytic, and antinociceptive effects, whereas the mitochondrial, redox, and anti-inflammatory actions, described almost exclusively in animal and cellular models, require substantially higher exposures and have not been demonstrated in surgical patients; the two arms are pharmacologically distinct and should not be pooled. Clinically, preoperative anxiolysis with melatonin in adults is the most consistently supported indication, whereas evidence for postoperative sleep, analgesia, delirium prevention, and organ protection remains heterogeneous and of low certainty. Most trials have used fixed clock-time dosing without measuring internal circadian phase or achieved plasma exposure, so null results cannot distinguish an ineffective mechanism from an inadequate intervention. The circadian-melatonin axis remains a plausible perioperative target, but clinical translation requires phase-aware, exposure-informed, and adequately powered trials.

articles.title: Progress in research on RAAS inhibitors regulating inflammatory responses and oxidative stress: from molecular mechanisms to clinical evidence.
articles.abstract: The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibitors serve as cornerstone pharmacotherapies for chronic conditions including hypertension, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease. Accumulating evidence over recent years has demonstrated that their target organ-protective effects cannot be fully attributed to blood pressure-lowering actions alone; instead, the modulation of inflammatory responses and oxidative stress emerges as a core mechanism underpinning their extra-antihypertensive benefits. However, systematic comparisons of such effects across distinct classes of RAAS inhibitors and integration of the latest evidence remain lacking. This review focuses on the molecular regulatory network of the dual RAAS axes, systematically dissecting the specific molecular mechanisms by which the canonical ACE-AngII-AT1R axis mediates tissue injury-via activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, NADPH oxidase, and NF-κB signaling pathways-while the protective ACE2-Ang(1-7)-MasR axis exerts anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects. A cross-class comparison is conducted to evaluate the divergent effects of five clinically prevalent RAAS inhibitor classes (ACE inhibitors [ACEI], angiotensin receptor blockers [ARB], direct renin inhibitors [DRI], angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors [ARNI], and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists [MRA]) on the regulation of inflammation and oxidative stress. By synthesizing the latest evidence from basic science and clinical studies over the past decade, we summarize the distinct organ-protective profiles of these agents across various target organs affected by cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, pulmonary disorders, neurological conditions, rheumatoid arthritis, and osteoporosis. Finally, addressing the limitations and inconsistencies within existing literature, this article proposes future research directions, strategies for optimizing combination therapies, and refined clinical trial designs to enhance the clinical application of RAAS inhibitors and facilitate the development of novel organ-protection paradigms.

articles.title: Virology-aware artificial intelligence for respiratory antiviral discovery: from molecular docking biases to RdRp-centered benchmarking.
articles.abstract: Respiratory RNA viruses remain a persistent threat because they combine high transmissibility, rapid evolution, immune escape, zoonotic spillover, and incomplete therapeutic coverage. RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRps) and polymerase complexes are among the most conserved and pharmacologically actionable viral targets, yet they are also challenging computational targets because their ligandable states depend on RNA templates, cofactors, divalent metals, multidomain architecture, and conformational transitions. Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), geometric deep learning (GDL), and generative molecular design are increasingly used to accelerate antiviral discovery, yet their performance is often inferred from general protein-ligand benchmarks dominated by non-viral targets. This review argues that respiratory RNA virus polymerases are a high-value but comparatively underrepresented class of antiviral targets and a complementary test case for evaluating AI-guided drug discovery. We synthesize current approaches in computer-aided drug design (CADD), molecular docking, ML-assisted virtual screening, molecular representations, pose-generation models, generative AI, and protein-ligand affinity benchmarking. We emphasize that docking scores, predicted affinity, and root-mean-square error (RMSE) values are insufficient unless linked to target engagement, enzymatic inhibition, cell-based antiviral activity, cytotoxicity, resistance, and pharmacological feasibility. We propose an RdRp-centered AI pipeline that integrates curated polymerase structural ensembles, leakage-resistant benchmarking, antiviral-specific evaluation tasks, ADME/Tox filtering, biochemical validation, cell-based infection assays, resistance profiling, and iterative model refinement. Moving beyond docking scores requires benchmarking models under virologically realistic conditions and validating whether computational prioritization enriches compounds with experimentally actionable antiviral activity.

articles.title: Digital Health Africa (DHA 2025) - Conference Report.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The Digital Health Africa 2025 Conference (DHA-2025, https://digitalhealthafrica.org/) addressed the integration of digital tools within critical global health priorities, including maternal and child health (MCH), antimicrobial resistance artificial intelligence (AI), and pharmacometrics. While the adoption of digital health shows immense potential for improving healthcare access in Africa's resource-limited environments, its practical application in the public sector remains sub-optimal due to policy misalignment and inadequate systemic investments. Digital health interventions can achieve sustained, large-scale impact when properly supported, as demonstrated by successful platforms like MomConnect in South Africa and MomCare in Kenya. However, successfully scaling these systems beyond initial pilots requires a robust foundation built on three pillars: technical capacity (infrastructure), legal legitimacy (regulation), and effective management (governance). Furthermore, while advanced tools like AI and pharmacometric modeling are now practical realities in healthcare in developed countries, the most significant challenge remains operationalizing and transitioning these sophisticated tools safely from the laboratory to the clinical bedside in Africa. CONCLUSION: Scientific advancement in digital health is insufficient on its own; the true test of innovation lies in its safe and practical integration into end-user healthcare delivery. To successfully scale digital health solutions in resource-constrained settings, stakeholders must prioritize cross-continental collaborations, invest heavily in capacity building, and secure long-term commitments to infrastructure and policy development.

articles.title: Andrographolide in hematological malignancies: potential mechanisms and translational challenges.
articles.abstract: Hematological malignancies comprise a heterogeneous group of life-threatening diseases arising from the hematopoietic system. Despite substantial advances in immunotherapies and molecularly targeted agents, drug resistance and disease relapse remain formidable clinical challenges. The natural product andrographolide, a diterpenoid lactone isolated from Andrographis paniculata, has attracted increasing research interest for its antitumor potential. This narrative review summarizes and discusses preclinical studies on andrographolide in hematological malignancies, covering its reported antitumor activities, drug synergy, and derivative development. Andrographolide has been reported to trigger intrinsic apoptosis through reactive oxygen species burst, while also suppressing STAT3 signaling via a ROS-dependent mechanism, thereby inducing tumor cell apoptosis. In addition, andrographolide has been reported to induce ferroptosis in a cell context-dependent manner, potentially through regulation of the p38/Nrf2/HO-1 pathway and upregulation of ACSL4 (also known as FACL4) expression; it also exerts anti-proliferative effects through metabolic reprogramming and induction of cellular differentiation. Andrographolide further suppresses inflammatory signaling in malignant cells through blockade of NF-κB signaling. In combination, andrographolide exhibits synergistic effects with cytarabine, vincristine, dexamethasone, and other agents in certain experimental settings. Finally, derivatives and analogs of andrographolide have also been explored.

articles.title: Macrophage lipophagy in atherosclerosis: from molecular mechanisms to traditional Chinese medicine interventions.
articles.abstract: Macrophage lipophagy, the selective autophagic degradation of intracellular lipid droplets, plays a central role in maintaining lipid homeostasis and has emerged as a promising therapeutic target for atherosclerosis (AS). This review systematically synthesizes the classification, molecular mechanisms, and key signaling networks of macrophage lipophagy. Moreover, recent evidence on the anti-AS effects of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) mediated by the regulation of macrophage lipophagy has also been summarized and evaluated, including active metabolites, medicinal plants, herbal formulas and commercial Chinese polyherbal preparations. Despite robust preclinical evidence, challenges remain. Significant efforts are still required to facilitate clinical translation and offer novel comprehensive strategies for the prevention and management of AS.

articles.title: Concomitant calcium supplementation does not compromise immunosuppressive dosing in kidney transplant recipients.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Polypharmacy following kidney transplantation entails a risk of both drug-drug interactions (DDIs) and reduced patient adherence. Co-administration of calcium supplementation and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) has previously been shown to influence pharmacokinetics (PK) of MMF. In current DDI databases, there is a recommendation for 2- to 3-h time-shifted administration. Whether a similar interaction potentially exists for tacrolimus has not been evaluated. We aimed to investigate the potential PK DDI between co-administrated calcium/vitamin D supplementation and the immunosuppressive drugs MMF and tacrolimus, using volumetric absorptive microsampling (VAMS). METHODS: Twenty-five kidney transplant recipients on stable MMF, tacrolimus and prednisolone treatment provided two 12-h PK investigations of simultaneous assessment of both mycophenolic acid (MPA) and tacrolimus concentrations. One PK investigation with and one without concomitant treatment with a calcium/vitamin D supplement. Capillary blood samples using VAMS were utilized to obtain samples in a patient friendly manner. Clinically relevant interactions were assessed by the with/without ratio of AUC0-12 and Cmax in accordance with EMA bioequivalence guidelines. RESULTS: The MPA AUC0-12 ratio was 0.94 (90% confidence interval [CI], 0.83-1.07) and the Cmax ratio was 0.79 (90% CI, 0.65-0.97). For tacrolimus, the AUC0-12 and Cmax ratios were 1.00 (90% CI, 0.92-1.09) and 0.96 (90% CI, 0.87-1.07), respectively. CONCLUSION: In kidney transplant recipients there is no clinically relevant PK DDI caused by concomitant administration of calcium/vitamin D supplementation with MMF and tacrolimus. Based on these observations, recommendation of time-shifted administration of calcium supplements and immunosuppressive drugs seems unnecessary.

articles.title: Development of a novel next-generation multi-epitope vaccine targeting the Guaroa virus glycoprotein precursor through reverse vaccinology.
articles.abstract: This study aimed to develop a multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Guaroa virus using integrated immunoinformatics and reverse vaccinology approaches. The viral glycoprotein precursor was selected as the target for epitope screening. Potential B-cell and T-cell epitopes with predicted antigenic properties, non-allergenicity, and non-toxicity were identified through computational analyses. Global population coverage assessment predicted a population coverage of 99.09% based on the selected HLA-associated epitopes. Selected epitopes were assembled into a chimeric vaccine construct containing β-defensin-3 adjuvant and linker sequences. Physicochemical analysis predicted properties relevant to solubility and recombinant expression, although these characteristics require experimental assessment. Structural prediction and refinement yielded a model in which 99.5% of residues were located within favored regions. Molecular docking predicted interactions between the vaccine construct and immune receptors TLR2, TLR3, and TLR4, with TLR4 showing the lowest docking score among the three receptors. Molecular dynamics simulations were used to assess the predicted structural behavior of the vaccine-receptor complexes. The vaccine-TLR4 complex yielded a docking score of -1212.9, while MM-GBSA analysis produced a ΔG_bind estimate of -227.14 kcal/mol based on the final trajectory frame. Immune simulation predicted increases in antibody production, cytokine release, and memory cell formation. Collectively, these findings support the computational prioritization of the construct as a vaccine candidate for further experimental investigation, although experimental and clinical validation remain necessary.

articles.title: Empirical linezolid target attainment in critically ill patients: integrating local susceptibility data and dosing strategies.
articles.abstract: Linezolid is important for treating infections caused by Gram-positive bacteria resistant to first-line agents. Severe infections often require empirical therapy before pathogen identification and susceptibility testing. This evaluation aims to compare different empirical linezolid dosing strategies in intensive care unit (ICU) patients to improve pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic target attainment while minimising toxicities. Three dosing strategies were compared: (i) standard dosing, (ii) therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM)-guided dosing, and (iii) a theoretical model-informed precision dosing (MIPD) strategy based on Bayesian forecasting with a population pharmacokinetic model. Each scenario was combined with an ICU-specific minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) distribution comprising more than 19,000 isolates collected over 10 years. Data from 117 critically ill patients with 2184 TDM samples were available. Linezolid resistance was highest in ICU isolates (9.6%) compared with isolates from the intermediate care unit (4.3%), general wards (3.6%), and emergency room (1.6%). Among ICU isolates, resistance increased significantly over the 10-year study period, from 6.3% in 2015 to 11.4% in 2024. Empirical target attainment was 36.6% with standard dosing and 48.5% with TDM-guided dose adaptation, in two different ICU cohorts that showed 35.9% and 59.4% baseline target attainment, respectively. Theoretical MIPD projected target attainment in 71.4-81.6% of patients. After excluding resistant isolates, the corresponding values were 40.5%, 53.7%, and 79.0-90.3%, respectively. Integrating a large contemporary ICU-specific MIC distribution with patient-level pharmacokinetic data, our results suggest MIPD may represent a promising strategy improving target attainment, in contrast to standard regimens and TDM-guided dosing which failed to achieve adequate target exposure in ICU patients.

articles.title: Cinobufagin induces peroxisome dysfunction through suppression of the peroxisomal biogenesis factor proteins and interferes with lipid metabolism to affect the growth of liver cancer cells.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Primary liver cancer is the sixth most commonly diagnosed cancer and the third most common cause of cancer death worldwide. Chansu is made by processing and drying the white serous fluid of the posterior ear and skin glands of Bufo bufo gargarizans Cantor or Bufo melanostictus Schneider. Chansu is a well-known traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) that is mainly used for detoxification, detumescence, analgesia, the treatment of cancer, and heart failure. Cinobufagin, as a bufadienolide, has been reported as the main antitumor active component of Chansu. However, the molecular mechanisms related to the anticancer effects of cinobufagin still remain elusive. PURPOSE: The purpose of this study is to explore whether cinobufagin inhibits the growth of HepG2 and SK-HEP-1 tumor cells by inducing peroxisome dysfunction and interfering with lipid metabolism. METHODS: The protein levels of catalase, ABCD3, PEX5, PEX6, and PEX10 in human hepatoma cells were analyzed by Western blotting. The effects of cinobufagin on the viability of HepG2 and SK-HEP-1 cells were detected by cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) assay and clone formation assay. Small interfering RNA (siRNA) transfection was used to explore whether inhibition of PEX could enhance the inhibitory effect of cinobufagin on cell growth of HepG2 and SK-HEP-1 tumor cells. The effects of cinobufagin on lipid metabolism were analyzed by untargeted metabolomics. The in vivo antitumor effects of cinobufagin were verified by animal studies. RESULTS: Cinobufagin causes peroxisome dysfunction in HepG2 and SK-HEP-1 tumor cells. From a mechanistic point of view, we reveal that cinobufagin downregulates the expression of PEX5, PEX10, and PEX6. In addition, through RNA interference, cinobufagin partially blocks the growth of HepG2 and SK-HEP-1 tumor cells and restrains the expression of lipid metabolism-related proteins via downregulating the expression of PEX5 and PEX10. Subsequently, we perform a non-targeted metabolomics analysis of the cells and find that cinobufagin exerts its anti-hepatoma effects by interfering with lipid metabolic reprogramming. The results show that cinobufagin mainly interferes with glycerophospholipid and fatty acyl levels. In addition, in vivo experiments reveal that cinobufagin restrains tumor growth without obvious adverse effects. Serum metabolomics analyses reveal that cinobufagin causes significant changes in the levels of lipid and lipid-like differential metabolites. CONCLUSION: Cinobufagin is a promising natural drug for the treatment of liver cancer, and PEXs may be potential molecular targets of cinobufagin to exert anticancer effects. Cinobufagin induces peroxisome dysfunction through suppression of the proteins encoded by the PEX genes and interferes with lipid metabolism to restrain the growth of liver cancer cells.

articles.title: Integrated in vitro and in silico assessment of antimicrobial, chemical antioxidant, and cytotoxic activities of endophytic Aspergillus sp. GK1 isolated from Mentha spicata roots.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Medicinal plants are a source of structurally diverse endophytic fungi which harbor significant pharmaceutical potential. METHODS: In the present research, the antimicrobial, chemical antioxidant, and cytotoxic properties of the ethyl acetate extract of endophytic Aspergillus sp. GK1 isolated from Mentha spicata roots were evaluated using both in vitro and in silico assessments. The crude extract was subjected to GC-MS profiling, which tentatively identified several metabolites, followed by molecular docking, drug-likeness, pharmacokinetic and toxicity prediction analyses. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION: The crude extract has shown broad spectrum antibacterial activity with inhibition zone of 15.66 ± 0.57 mm against Escherichia coli, 14.66 ± 1.52 mm against Staphylococcus aureus, 14.00 ± 0.00 mm against Staphylococcus epidermidis and 13.33 ± 0.57 mm against Bacillus subtilis. Minimum inhibitory concentration values were 16, 32, 64, and 64 μg/mL, while minimum bactericidal concentration values were 32, 32, 64, and 128 μg/mL, respectively. The extract showed concentration-dependent responses in chemical antioxidant assays, including DPPH radical-scavenging, hydrogen peroxide-scavenging, reducing-power and total antioxidant-capacity assays. A strong correlation between chemical antioxidant capacity and total phenolics (R2 = 0.9752-0.9986) and total flavonoids (R2 = 0.9814-0.9956) content was found. The extract exhibited concentration-dependent cytotoxicity against MCF-7 cells with an IC50 value of 69.20 μg/mL that had positive correlation with the phenolics and flavonoids content. The analysis of GC-MS points to the presence of several metabolites, including 2-Buten-1-one, 1,3-diphenyl- (dypnone, a β-methyl2-Buten-1-one, 1,3-diphenyl-; CID 95329) which showed the highest binding affinity to selected protein targets, along with favourable drug-likeness, in silico pharmacokinetic and toxicity properties. The extract demonstrated antibacterial activity, measurable chemical antioxidant/ radical-scavenging properties, and cytotoxic effects under the experimental conditions. Integrated experimental and computational studies highlighted the tentatively identified 2-Buten-1-one, 1,3-diphenyl- as a compound of interest for further investigation. CONCLUSION: These findings provide preliminary indication for the possible biological activity of the Aspergillus sp. GK1 extract and support further bioassay- guided fractionation, isolation, structural characterization, mechanistic studies, and in vivo analysis of its active constituents.

articles.title: Model-informed precision dosing of vancomycin and amikacin in critically ill neonates: a pre- and post-intervention study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Optimal antimicrobial dosing in neonates is complicated by extreme developmental pharmacokinetic (PK) variability. Traditional therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) fails to achieve PK/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) target attainment in this vulnerable population. OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether implementation of Bayesian model-informed precision dosing (MIPD) improved PK/PD target attainment and exposure dose adjustment compared with conventional TDM in critically ill neonates. METHODS: This pre- and post-intervention design comparing a historical retrospective cohort with a prospective MIPD validation single-center cohort study included 61 neonates receiving vancomycin or amikacin. An initial observational phase with standard dosing (n = 30) was followed by an intervention phase (n = 31) using Bayesian dose adjustment. Secondary outcomes included acute nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, infection-related inflammatory biomarkers (ΔCRP and ΔProcalcitonin), illness severity (ΔSNAPPE-II), and the treatment-duration-to-hospital-length-of-stay ratio (DOT/LOS) in NICU. RESULTS: Regarding posterior model concordance, agreement for vancomycin was limited, as evidenced by an overall mean absolute error (MAE) of 5.47 mg/L. For amikacin, concordance was modest (overall MAE: 8.96 mg/L; median absolute error [MdAE]: 1.31 mg/L), reflecting persistent modeling challenges. For vancomycin, therapeutic target attainment was higher with MIPD than with standard dosing (5/30, 16.7% vs. 1/26, 3.8%). Similarly for amikacin, therapeutic target attainment was higher in the MIPD group (10/27, 37.0% vs. 5/26, 19.2%). In an exploratory secondary analysis, ΔSNAPPE-II differed between the standard dosing and MIPD cohorts (-2.5 vs. 0; p = 0.040), favoring standard dosing; as SNAPPE-II is not validated for longitudinal monitoring and the design was non-randomized, this does not constitute evidence of clinical benefit for either strategy. For the overall combined cohort, DOT/LOS was significantly lower in the MIPD group (p = 0.043). No differences in the rates of acute kidney injury (6.9% vs. 10.0%, p = 1.000) or ototoxicity (8.0% vs. 7.1%, p = 1.000) were detected, although the study was underpowered to rule out clinically important differences. CONCLUSION: Bayesian MIPD was associated with numerically but not statistically higher pharmacodynamic target attainment (AUC/MIC and Cmax/MIC) for vancomycin and amikacin, and no improvement in clinical outcomes was demonstrated. While amikacin modeling requires further refinement, adequately powered trials are needed to definitively assess the impact of MIPD on safety and clinical outcomes.
